title: Temiya the silent prince
hookLine: a prince pretends to be mute for sixteen years rather than rule by punishment
last: VESSANTARA'S CHILDREN — THE TRADITION ARGUES TOO.

lines: FROM OUTSIDE, THEY LOOK THE SAME.
A BABY ON A KING'S LAP.
cards: A meeting ends, and one person never said a word. Was it wisdom? Was it fear?
From the outside, the two look exactly the same. Today's story is about a silence so long and so stubborn that everyone decided the silent one was broken. He wasn't.
He was choosing. It's the Temiya Jataka, number 538, the first of the ten long Jatakas that close the collection, and it starts with a baby on a king's lap.

teach.b: The baby is Temiya, the long-awaited son of the king of Benares. Still only an infant, he sits on his father's lap while the king judges prisoners, and he watches his father order terrible punishments.
And the story says the baby remembers: in a past life he was a king too, and the harsh judgments he handed down led him to long suffering afterward. He's terrified. He does not want this throne.
A goddess who lives in the royal parasol gives him advice: pretend you can't speak, can't hear, can't walk. So he does.
For sixteen years. The court tries everything to catch him out: sweets he could reach for, frightening noises, fire, snakes. Every test, the story says, he stays still.
Finally the advisers tell the king this son is bad luck, and the king orders him taken out and buried. The charioteer drives him to the forest and starts to dig.

Then Temiya stands up, walks, lifts the chariot, and speaks. He tells the charioteer why he kept silent, and he chooses the life of a forest ascetic. In the end his parents and much of the kingdom come out and follow him.
In the tradition, this life is linked with nekkhamma, renunciation: leaving behind the power that would have made him cruel.
His silence wasn't weakness, or sulking. It was a refusal. He would not say the words that condemn.

how: The Temiya story is told as the first of the ten great Jatakas, and in Thailand and elsewhere it's painted on temple walls; Buddhists link it with the perfection of renunciation.

o: a goddess living in the royal parasol
a prince who truly couldn't speak or hear
the prince who chose silence over the throne

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: judged prisoners with his son on his lap

s: he chose silence for sixteen years, then stood up and spoke to the charioteer.
the Temiya Jataka is the first of the ten long Jatakas
the ten great births begin with Temiya and end with Vessantara.
his silence was about refusing to rule by punishment
he had seen what harsh judgments led to, and would not take the throne.

games.q: you're Temiya, sixteen years silent, and the charioteer is digging your grave. what do you do?
games.why: he stands, lifts the chariot, and tells the charioteer why. then he chooses the forest, not the throne.

practice: Be silent on purpose, and listen; let the sounds of the room come to you: a hum, traffic, your own breath.
Inside, the talking may keep going, replies, rehearsals, arguments with people who aren't here, and you don't need to stop it.
Just decline to follow it, the way Temiya declined the throne, and come back to the sounds and the breath.

wordCard.voice: Temiya. The prince who kept silent for sixteen years rather than rule by punishment.
